cipher-grid.intro_html:
Clavis Polygraphiae (1518 (companion key), [Oppenheim]) -- Cipher-grid tables (Style C)

Source witness: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB) München, via MDZ digital library. Standalone Clavis (key). The substitution tables here are the same scheme as in the Polygraphia VI editions, but presented for direct decipherment use.

What you are looking at

These chunks render Trithemius's tabular ciphers -- structurally different from the verbal-substitution columns of the cipher-key set. Three families recur:

  • Expansion-figure matrices (Prima / Secunda / Tertia / Quarta figura expansionis tabulae) -- bigram-pair tables and alphabet-rotation grids that derive new alphabets from a base alphabet by transposition.
  • Orchema numerale -- a 24x24 numerical-substitution matrix in Polygraphia VI book six, indexed by Latin letters on both axes with numbers 6-29 in the body. Trithemius's own note describes the diagonals as an 'infinite leap' (transversaliter a quatuor angulis).
  • Spirit-army hierarchies -- positional tables of demonic ranks (Oriens / Duxes majoris / Duxes minoris / Subduces) from the Steganographia tradition; structurally tabular but not a cipher in the strict substitution-table sense.

How the renderer chose its layout

Each source section is tokenised row-by-row. When most rows have the same cell count (and that count is <= 28), the renderer emits a markdown table; otherwise it preserves the source layout as a fenced code block. Trithemius's own commentary (where it appears in long Latin prose between figures) is lifted out into a blockquote. -- marks an OCR-illegible cell.

Honest limits

  • Identical-rows artefact: the printed Polygraphia VI expansion figures display Caesar-rotated alphabets, but the OCR frequently linearises them to identical rows (each row = the plain alphabet). The renderer surfaces what the OCR sees; the original rotation is recoverable only by inspecting the facsimile image.
  • Header detection is heuristic: lines matching figure-header patterns are lifted out, but a header buried in continuous prose may be missed.
  • This work contributes 11 cipher-grid chunks.

Provenance

Auto-generated from the OCR'd source by scripts/render_style_cipher_grid.py. Phase 0.5 manual reclassification moved 43 expansion-figure chunks from cipher-key to cipher-grid (see scripts/reclassify_expansion_figures.py).

cipher-key.intro_html:
Clavis Polygraphiae (1518 (companion key), [Oppenheim]) — Cipher tables

Source witness: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB) München, via MDZ digital library. Standalone Clavis (key). The substitution tables here are the same scheme as in the Polygraphia VI editions, but presented for direct decipherment use.

What you are looking at

The Clavis Polygraphiae is Johannes Trithemius's exposition of substitution cipher technique, originally dedicated to Maximilian I in 1508. Each of the six books presents a different modus of enciphering plaintext as a sequence of Latin words. The basic mechanism is constant across modi:

  • The plaintext is broken into individual letters.
  • Each letter is replaced by a Latin word drawn from a substitution column (the alphabetum of cipher words).
  • For multi-column modi, the substitution rotates with the letter's position: position 1 uses column 1, position 2 uses column 2, and so on, returning to column 1 once the sequence exhausts.
  • The cipher words are chosen so that any ordinary plaintext produces a grammatical Latin sentence — invariably a devotional invocation. The ciphertext is thus undetectable: it reads as ordinary monastic prayer.

Worked example — Modus Primus, eight-column substitution

To encipher the eight-letter plaintext ABCDEFGH using Modus Primus (the first cipher of Liber Septimus / Clavis Polygraphiae, eight substitution columns):

pos plain col cipher-word
1 A C1 facti
2 B C2 Certe
3 C C3 timendum
4 D C4 continue
5 E C5 sempiternum
6 F C6 fabricatorem
7 G C7 supercaelestium
8 H C8 compassionem

The resulting ciphertext reads:

Facti certe timendum continue sempiternum fabricatorem supercaelestium compassionem.

"[We have] truly been made, [to be] continually feared the eternal fashioner of the heavenly ones, by compassion."

To an eavesdropper this is an ordinary Latin devotional sentence. Only the recipient who knows to take the n-th letter of the n-th word's enciphering column recovers the plaintext ABCDEFGH.

How to read the table files

The substitution columns from this work's source are rendered per chunk under translations/style-c-cipher-key/full/. This work contributes 65 cipher-key chunks; 64 parse cleanly into Style C tables and 1 fall back to a verbatim source rendering (see Honest limits below).

Each chunk file:

  • Identifies the source chunk (e.g. full_chunk_0025).
  • States the per-page-section detected patterns:
  • A — one entry per line (single substitution column, or several columns concatenated on one page).
  • B — two or three columns interleaved per line (a X a Y or a X a Y a Z), with optional trailing source line-numbers.
  • D — letter plus several numeric cipher values per line.
  • Renders an alphabet-down / columns-across markdown table aligned by Trithemius's 24-letter alphabet (a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t v x y z w, omitting j and u), plus an optional 25th zu / zv / tv slot for the v-ligature.

Honest limits

  • OCR scannos are preserved as-they-appear in cell values (e.g. Vtigiz for Vtique, fabricatosem for fabricatorem, pissislimum for piissimum). The v1 parser repairs positional OCR errors in the letter markers (long-s misread as f; 2v misread for zv; iv/lv for zv) but does not repair content — that is a translation-quality problem (handled by the GPT-5.5 audit pipeline), not a layout problem.
  • Dropped column markers: where a row had its column marker dropped by OCR (e.g. a misericordislima factorem instead of a misericordislima a factorem), the parser splits the value into N equal pieces when N matches the section's modal cells-per-row, and leaves the value merged otherwise.
  • Letter-marker repair via positional alignment: when a column is near-full (≥ 18 entries), each entry's letter marker is rewritten to its positional canonical alphabet slot. This catches the common long-s/f confusion (where row s was rendered as f by the OCR) but assumes the column traverses the alphabet sequentially from a.
  • Wide multi-alphabet tables: a subset of chunks (1 of 65 for this work) hold very wide octo-modus tables that the v1 parser cannot sub-split into individual columns. These fall back to a verbatim rendering of the source OCR, with a comment indicating the parser's limit.

Provenance

Auto-generated from the OCR'd source by scripts/render_style_cipher_key.py and scripts/build_cipher_book_intro.py. The OCR pipeline, manual chunk reclassification (Phase 0.5), and GPT-5.5 audit are documented in data/corpus/_PHASE_05_FINDINGS.md and METHODOLOGY_GPT_AUDIT.md. This Style C rendering is one of the four content-type rendering styles chosen for the crypto-occult cluster after the 2026-05-30 Phase 1 specimen review.

prose-damaged.intro_html:
About These Review Renderings

These passages preserve damaged prose rather than smoothing it into false certainty. They keep OCR loss, embedded cipher tenors, and conjectural readings visible so readers can compare them against the Latin and source scan.

They should be treated as review renderings, not certified final editions.

chunks.name: full_chunk_0001
chunks.html:
Clavis Polygraphiae — damage-preserving rendering, full_chunk_0001

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: mid_damage_recoverable; OCR quality: 2/5.

Audit note — It treated a damaged provenance/portrait area as a dedication and 1563 imprint; the recoverable title is the 1518 Polygraphia addressed to Maximilian.

Style C Translation: Clavis Polygraphiae Front Matter Fragment

Pages 001-005

Modern Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbüttel digitization notices, citation instructions, and gray-scale targets; these are not Trithemian Latin prose and contain no cipher tenor.

Page 006

Appendix: 1518.

Page 007

[Provenance or ownership line:] Ferdinand Albert, [conjectured: Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg].^1

Six Books of the Polygraphy,^2 by Johannes Trithemius,^3 abbot of Peapolis,^4 formerly of Spanheim,^5 addressed to Emperor Maximilian.^6

With favor and privilege [conjectured: of the Imperial Majesty].^7

Johannes Trithemius.^3

A lower caption or subscription after the portrait is [unclear].^8

^1. The OCR “Ferdinando Alberto Dux Frangiscalis et Vicenburgensis” is not a secure dedication formula. “Brunsvicensis et Luneburgensis” is a defensible reconstruction from the ducal style of Brunswick-Lüneburg; the problem is OCR/provenance damage, not authorial obscurity. ^2. Polygraphia: Trithemius’s cryptographic/steganographic “many-writing” work; here the title is not a prose sentence but title-page matter. ^3. Johannes Trithemius (1462-1516), Benedictine abbot and author. The repeated “IO. TRITHEMIVS” is likely a portrait caption/name, not a new imprint statement. ^4. Peapolis is Trithemius’s humanist Latin for Würzburg; “abbas Peapolitanus” means abbot at St James/Würzburg, not Naples. This is an uncommon place-name, not an OCR correction. ^5. Spanheimensis: of Sponheim/Spanheim, Trithemius’s former abbey. ^6. Maximilianus Caesar: Emperor Maximilian I. Latin “ad” means “addressed to / for,” not necessarily a separate personal dedication on this damaged leaf. ^7. The OCR “Lum gratia et privilegio L. OS.” is best read as a damaged “Cum gratia et privilegio C.M.” or similar privilege formula; C.M. would abbreviate Caesarea Maiestas, “Imperial Majesty.” OCR scannos affect initial C/L and abbreviation letters. ^8. The supplied OCR “Lyvolis 1563. m. gris. 2. Ruckius” is not recoverable as Latin from this excerpt and should not be treated silently as a 1563 imprint. Bibliographic controls identify the edition as [Basel]: Haselberg, 1518; see HAB record http://diglib.hab.de/drucke/fb-128/start.htm and LOC record https://www.loc.gov/item/32017914/.

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: heavy_damage_partial; OCR quality: 3/5.

Audit note — The v1.0 normalized many damaged OCR forms into fluent historical claims, especially “bubones,” “latibulum,” numerals, and the Charlemagne sentence, without marking uncertainty.

Style C Translation: Clavis Polygraphiae, p. 018 Fragment

Frankish King and Clodius

The most powerful king of the Franks^1 in Germany, in the [conjectured: four-hundred-and-twenty-fourth]^2 year of the Lord’s nativity, when he [conjectured: entered]^3 the borders of the Gauls^4 in force, in order that all things might be done in complete safety, bound foreign minutiae^5 to his secrets.

Clodius the Long-haired,^6 the elder-by-birth son of Pharamund,^7 succeeding his father in the kingship of the Franks, afterward willingly subjected the whole of Gaul to himself and to his rule. He ordered all the Gauls, as conquered men and slaves, to be stripped of their hair and their beards shaved; but he commanded the Franks, conquerors and masters of the Gauls, to let their hair and beard grow. Hence he too was called “the Long-haired.” In imitation of his race, he wrapped the mysteries of his counsel^8 in signs both his own and foreign.

Charlemagne

Charles the Great^9 by surname, [conjectured: the sixty-third]^10 after Marcomer,^11 king of the Franks, who was the first of the Franks to rule the Romans,^12 having Nanno the grammarian^13 as his teacher, and wishing to adorn with grammatical rules the beginnings of Latin in the German language, which was his paternal tongue, undertook a difficult work. Yet, entangled in many matters and overtaken by delay, he did not complete it. But he bound [unclear: bubones?]^14 to various and many minutiae; [unclear], than whom Brabant^15 had no greater [conjectured: native?], nor Germany one at Namur.^16 To the individual prefects of the kingdom he entrusted individual [unclear: bubones?] by art.

Normans and Bede

The Normans,^17 having gone out from the borders of the Goths,^18 when they once cruelly laid waste Gaul, summoned also [unclear: Greek bubones?] and prepared a safe [conjectured: hiding-place / gibbet?]^19 for their secrets, which today is known to few.

Our Bede,^20 a monk in England, not ignorant of the [unclear: secrets? stuffing?]^21 of the Normans, found many things like these in the writings and inventions of the ancients, by which they made a dark path into mysteries. He himself first commended astrology^22 to the memory of posterity, and invented dactylology.^23

There were some who discerned minutiae by visible accidents,^24 for whom prudence did not fear night in the day, and, without the ministry of [unclear: bubones?], light shone in darkness.

Steganography and Later Arts

Concerning these matters of our Steganography,^25 because a certain illustrious count palatine and prince-elector^26 made inquiry, he caused clear documents to be approved for us by experiment. Others, however, multiplying rules by the division of minutiae, [unclear] the schemes of nature back to the beginnings of the barbarians, [unclear] in darkness the shadow-dances^27 of those being born; and where the secrecy of counsel required it, by [conjectured: diagrams]^28 it supplied a cabala^29 to the absent. Great labor lies in these things, and long exercise of a sharp mind; in this no one suddenly becomes skilled at first sight. Necessity suffices for all things.

There were also those whom celestial harmony^30 taught to compose foreign utterances: for those who understood, the vision of these was twofold, while the one [conjectured: held the sense in suspense], the other lifted the mind into the ether. God can do all things. Many have tried to seek light in shadow without light, but by no means could they, because the fire now lies buried in ashes. Some, practiced painters of masks,^31 divided [unclear: twenty?] one into two [unclear: at a point], of whom one [unclear: mirophos] in [unclear].

^1. “Francorũ” = Francorum. OCR abbreviation expansion; named people of the Franks. ^2. OCR “quadragesimaetimo uicefimo quarto” is not grammatical as printed; likely a damaged numeral such as “quadringentesimo vicesimo quarto,” i.e. 424. ^3. OCR “in traraet” is probably “intraret.” Positional spacing and letter confusion. ^4. “Gallorum” / Gauls; historical-ethnic vocabulary. ^5. “minutiae” is retained as a technical steganographic/cipher term in this passage; it seems to denote small units, signs, or cipher elements. ^6. Clodius Crinitus, a legendary/early Frankish ruler; “Crinitus” means long-haired. ^7. Pharamund/Pharamond, legendary king of the Franks; OCR “Pharamidi” for Pharamundi. ^8. “mysteria consilii” is secrecy/counsel vocabulary; in Trithemius this often shades into steganographic concealment. ^9. OCR “Caro Ius Magnus” = Carolus Magnus, Charlemagne. ^10. OCR “faxegeminus” is likely a scanno for a numeral such as “sexagesimus”; the exact ordinal remains uncertain. ^11. Marcomer/Marcomir, legendary Frankish ancestor or ruler. ^12. “Imperavit Romanis” refers to Charlemagne’s imperial rule over Romans/the Roman Empire. ^13. “Nannone grammatico” may refer to an otherwise uncertain grammarian; the name is preserved but should be checked against the print. ^14. OCR repeatedly gives “bubones” / “bur bonibus” / “But bones.” It may be a scanno or a deliberately odd cipher term; not safely normalized. ^15. Brabant, historical region in the Low Countries. ^16. Namur, city/region in present-day Belgium; OCR syntax around this phrase is badly damaged. ^17. Normans; historical-military people. ^18. “Goths” here is ethnic/geographical vocabulary, possibly legendary ethnography. ^19. OCR “laibulum” could be “latibulum” (hiding-place) or, less likely, “patibulum” (gibbet); context favors “latibulum,” but the reading is not secure. ^20. Bede, the English monk and scholar. ^21. OCR “far ci” is not secure; possibly a scanno for a word meaning secrets, art, or practice. ^22. Astrology as a learned/technical art. ^23. Dactylology: finger-sign language or finger-reckoning/signing, a technical communication term. ^24. “accidentia visibilia” are visible accidental features/signs; scholastic and technical vocabulary. ^25. Steganography: Trithemius’s art of hidden writing; OCR “fleganographie” for steganographiae. ^26. “comes palatinus princeps elector” = count palatine and prince-elector, likely the Palatine elector; named title, not identified further from this fragment. ^27. OCR “orchemata” resembles Greek-derived “orchemata,” dances; phrase remains authorially obscure and OCR-damaged. ^28. OCR “diapryamata” may point to “diagrammata,” diagrams, but the reading is conjectural. ^29. Cabala/Kabbalah, esoteric technical term; here probably a method of concealed communication to absentees. ^30. “harmonia coelestis,” celestial harmony; theological/esoteric cosmological vocabulary. ^31. “larvarum pictores,” painters of masks/phantoms; obscure, possibly a cipher-art metaphor rather than literal painters.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Page 019: Damage-Preserving Translation

Page 019

[Unclear] lies hidden in darkness; the other, however, a philosopher who loves the light,^1 hates darkness and loves light; he has hidden the secret under the owl.^2 Rufus and Bede^3 were [unclear], among certain men, whose intention, advancing toward wider matters, bound together in things many items more useful and more venerable, though useless to the eyes of all; and no less did it compel stones and [conjectured: fruits], things that lack voices, to speak with a human tongue.

Why should I bring in brute creatures,^4 to whose art the rest obey? This secret [unclear: they find / all find]; they rightly prefer [unclear] to all things. Through it the eyes of [unclear] are strengthened, and yet reason bids one shrink from great things to small things, and by no means commit pearls to swine.^5 From nothing, nothing is brought back.

Note that the multitude of useful things is great; to us, however, they remain useless and remote unless [unclear] are fitted to them as preliminaries. Then the illuminated mind of man^6 would recognize and discover wonders. But to treat these things more fully is not part of the present undertaking; that requires another work, of greater and weightier [unclear], and [conjectured: another] time.

Matthias of Hungary,^7 [conjectured: king / powerful in rule], and harder than adamant, [conjectured: hammer of the Turks],^8 who by no [unclear] discovered many things and [unclear] of the cross,^9 things wonderful to all by foresight, talent, and art; he found many more things, adorned owls with ornate periphrases,^10 and [conjectured: kept] his mysteries, the secrets of manifold variety. But [unclear] made manifest by flowing industry. Wisdom prevailed over gold; in its own [unclear: time] [unclear] triumphed in glories.

[Unclear] the wise man, empty fame, in [unclear: heart / basket] well [unclear], because from the desire of understanding higher things, future deeds, and through the [unclear: subtlety / futility] of the binary,^11 they return from the ternary^12 into unity,^13 and thereafter are joined in turn to the denary.^14 Pythagoras,^15 [conjectured: the Samian], instructed his disciples [unclear] concerning the joining-on of the quaternary,^16 in which the first principle of numbering is contained. Count thus by this method: one, two, three, four. If you are sound in mind, you have the tenth. The denary is the seed of perfection [unclear]. What is eleven, if not the denary and unity? What is twenty? Twice ten. What is thirty? Three times ten. What is forty? Four times ten; you have also the quaternary. [Unclear] you have gone back. And what is a hundred, except ten times ten? Deep is the mystery of this doctrine, and it has been manifest to few.

For love of brevity we pass over many who, flourishing by nature and art, applied prudence to secret things,^17 and what seemed impossible to many in their necessities, [unclear] easily brought forth into use. A cultivated mind [unclear] great things; and the one who clings to God^18 becomes, by understanding, another world. Many are the mysteries of kingship,^19 and counsels [unclear] with ingenious cares, in which both [conjectured: counsel] and faith are required; and it is harmful to believe rare things, while doubt joined with [unclear] admits [unclear: fenced-off matters].

Therefore it would have been worth the labor that all leading men [conjectured: be philosophers], and also [conjectured: skilled in languages and lapidary art],^20 supported, fortified, [unclear], and marked by protections, so that they themselves should neither wish to deceive others, nor be easily able to be supplanted by another. [Conjectured: Prudence] alone,^21 as a supporting companion, makes the prince glorious.

^1. “philosophos” is probably an OCR or grammatical deformation for a singular philosopher/philosophus; the light/darkness antithesis is clear, but the exact syntax is damaged. ^2. “bubone” / “bubones” literally “owl(s)”; in this cipher-preface context it may be a technical cover-sign or emblem, not merely a bird. OCR “cultidit” likely for “condidit” or a similar verb of hiding. ^3. “Rufus Beda” is read cautiously as Rufus and Bede. Bede may be the Venerable Bede, but the damaged context does not securely identify either figure. ^4. “bruta” means dumb/brute creatures; the following “caeta” is likely OCR for “cetera,” “the rest.” ^5. Allusion to Matthew 7:6, “pearls before swine.” The Latin “comiterre” is likely OCR for “committere.” ^6. “mens hominis illuminata” is clear enough: an enlightened or illuminated human mind, with theological-philosophical coloring. ^7. “Mathias Vngaria” likely refers to Matthias Corvinus, king of Hungary, but the title and surrounding praise are damaged. ^8. “mallens turcari” is plausibly OCR for “malleus Turcarum,” “hammer of the Turks,” a military epithet; this is a conjecture from context and letter-shape confusion. ^9. “crucis” is legible as “of the cross,” but its syntactic role is unrecoverable here. ^10. “periphrastibus ornatis” appears to mean “with ornate periphrases”; this is technical rhetorical/cipher vocabulary, since periphrasis can function as concealment. ^11. “binar[unclear]” refers to the binary or dyad; whether the source says “subtlety” or “futility” before it is not secure. ^12. “ternario” is the ternary/triad, part of the numerological sequence. ^13. “unitate” is unity/oneness, a standard metaphysical and numerical term. ^14. “denarii” is the denary/decad, central to the following Pythagorean numerology. ^15. “Pythagoras” is clear. The damaged “S[unclear]itas” may conceal “Samius,” “the Samian.” ^16. “quaternarii” is conjectured from the sequence one-two-three-four and the later “quaternam”; the source OCR has “quaenerarii.” ^17. “arcanis” are secrets or hidden arts; in this work the word also belongs to the vocabulary of cryptographic concealment. ^18. “adhernet deo” is a scanno for “adhaeret Deo,” “clings/adheres to God.” ^19. “mysteria regae” is likely “mysteria regia/regni,” mysteries of kingship or royal secrets; exact case is damaged. ^20. “lapidaria” may refer to lapidary art or lore of stones; the surrounding words about languages and training are badly OCR-damaged. ^21. “Sola praedicit” is likely not “alone foretells”; a more plausible damaged reading is “sola prudentia,” “prudence alone,” given the prior ethical-political context. This remains conjectural.

Clavis Polygraphiae — damage-preserving rendering, full_chunk_0015

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: heavy_damage_partial; OCR quality: 3/5.

Audit note — V1.0 repeatedly normalized damaged cipher terminology into smooth prose, especially the monad/binary/ternary and table passages, without marking conjectural restorations.

Style C Translation: Clavis Polygraphiae, Indices to Books III-V

Index of the things which [conjectured: the third] book of the Polygraphy contains^1

In the third book of the Polygraphy, after crossing the prescribed boundaries of our nation [unclear: or mode/reason of speech], we are led to foreign things; and, being set in the midst of the French in an [unclear: essential/native] way,^2 we wander further through the images and likenesses of barbarian peoples.^3 For with almost four thousand mythological phrase-units^4 set in order by art, we very easily show the force of an artificial unity,^5 and how symbolic signs,^6 with their own binary, may conceal it more safely at every time. Here the binary is harder for unity; and unless our philologist is made sharp-sighted by prudence, he will render the binary as contrary to the monad.^7 For only the ternary, which proceeds from unity and the binary, [unclear: gives/contains] in itself the [unclear] of both.^8 What if the necessary usefulness of the method^9 is extended beyond the bounds of the proposed matter, and so many paraphrases^10 were to strive through the minutes from the beginning of the day, until the minute establishes the degree at which night [unclear: equals] day? The face of this image [unclear: knows the favor/propitiousness] of silence; it does not fear the frauds of [unclear]. However greatly you wish to extend the supply, it is varied without end.

Index, or [unclear: depiction/painting], of the things treated in the fourth book

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy we have much more fully brought the binary, a matter beset by many obstacles, back to unity at first sight and without laborious difficulties. Hence we use a circle^11 in great matters, a line or point in the smallest. Nor does it matter whether [unclear: day] does not surpass [unclear], or whether light does not yield to darkness, because the circle admits no end, and fullness is not admired in empty things. For they are contraries, and when one succeeds, the other is corrupted by the other. The singular mystery of the binary code^12 is transmitted in this fourth book of the Polygraphy, while [unclear: the old copyist/older abundance itself] otherwise [unclear] more copiously, unless it is marked in the height by the binary. But in that part, among [unclear: owls/obscurities], lightness is for us [unclear] in difficult suspicions. The joining-together of this matter makes paraphrases from infinite atoms.

Index, or [unclear: depiction/painting], of the things treated in the fifth book

In the fifth book of the Polygraphy, the letters of the Latins,^13 which we Germans also use,^14 [are arranged] in order in two tables, of which one is called [conjectured: the straight table], and the other [conjectured: the inverse].^15 To these we have added [unclear: old arrangements/figures], so that in foreign matters, and with less labor than in open ones, we may seem to work without difficulty. For besides those things which have been placed by us in plain sight, many more still lie hidden in the inner secrets; through them a way is opened for the understanding operator^16 toward greater things than those which are put before the eyes of the unskilled. We have also added [unclear: universal grammar/rules], by which, according to our will, hidden things may become manifest. Hence, through the [unclear: full/formal] operation of this book, all [unclear: beginnings/unknown things] are safely handed over to cabalistic methods,^17 although the mysteries [unclear: are protected/are made new] from the suspicion of [unclear]. For the very form of the metathesis of signs^18 generates suspicion in the beholder, though no harm was present in it for [unclear: owls/the ignorant]. But you, once you have attained the understanding of this work, will easily penetrate every metathesis of letters among our people and among the Latins.

^1. The heading is damaged: “textu” likely conceals “tertio,” and “continet indicet” points to an index formula, but the exact printed syntax is not recoverable from the OCR alone. ^2. “Francoru effentáli coëstití” is probably “Francorum ... constituti”; the adjective/adverb is uncertain. This likely concerns French-language material in Book III. ^3. OCR “filiúdines bar baronú lógiús cuagamur” is recoverable as “similitudines barbarorum longius vagamur.” “Barbarian” here means non-Latin/foreign, not necessarily savage. ^4. “phra[m]atib[?]” appears to be “phrasmatibus/phrasematis,” phrase-units or formulaic expressions used for polygraphic substitution. ^5. “unitas artificialis” is technical cipher language: an artificial unifying system for diverse signs or phrases. ^6. “notíes” likely for “notae,” signs/marks, not “notions” in the modern abstract sense. ^7. Monad/binary/ternary are numerical and cipher-theoretical terms here, with possible Neoplatonic coloring; the OCR around “unitati binariis” is syntactically damaged. ^8. The clause “et[?] palidrom[?] in fe dôneçit utríusq” is not safely emendable. “palidrom” may be an OCR scanno for a technical term, but “palindrome” should not be silently imposed. ^9. “róis” may stand for “rationis”; translation “method” is contextual and marked by the surrounding cipher vocabulary. ^10. “paraphrasmata” are cipher paraphrases or phrase expansions, not ordinary rhetorical paraphrase only. ^11. Circle, line, and point are technical graphic/cipher devices in this section, not merely metaphors. ^12. “binarii codicis” or similar: the binary code/book/system. The source’s “códícis” is clear enough, but surrounding syntax is damaged. ^13. “latinoru Íras” is almost certainly “Latinorum literas,” the Latin alphabet. ^14. “nos Germani” is not a hidden German tenor; it is an overt Latin statement that Germans use the Latin letters. ^15. OCR “re[?]ta” and “auera” plausibly conceal “recta” and “aversa/inversa,” the straight and reversed tables; these are conjectural but contextually strong. ^16. “intelligenti operatori” is probably intended: the practitioner who understands the system. ^17. “cabalisticis” reflects Trithemius’s technical/esoteric vocabulary for hidden writing; it should not be normalized into ordinary “cryptographic” without note. ^18. “metathesis signorum/literarum” means transposition or rearrangement of signs/letters, a technical cipher operation.

chunks.html:
Clavis Polygraphiae — damage-preserving rendering, full_chunk_0017

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: heavy_damage_partial; OCR quality: 2/5.

Audit note — V1 repeatedly normalizes damaged syntax into smooth Latin, especially the opening benefits and the Bartholomaeus anecdote, masking major OCR uncertainty as certain prose.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Preface / Decipherment Commentary, Page 027

[conjectured: Whoever] has learned to read and write in his mother tongue^1 is taught, under the Latin language, how to write as he wishes, elegantly and [conjectured: concisely]; how by solitary [conjectured: notes]^2 to conceal and hide the secrets of his hidden signifying-system^3; how, by whatever silent art^4 he chooses, to announce matters very widely, safely, securely, and without suspicion; and likewise to forewarn [unclear], so that they may not be understood by others [unclear]. This we promise.

The third benefit is that to one unskilled in Roman speech^5 we promise that in a few hours he will not only [conjectured: be able] to write and read, but also to understand, if he prudently applies the duty of the office; this we have judged should not be rejected without reasonable cause. For the novice pupil of this new art^6 will write what he had known in his own language, and, once it has been governed by instruction in the Latin tongue, [conjectured: he will understand the cosmopolitan/interpreted speech], if you take it word by word; that will suffice for use. Finally, this instruction can be enlarged to all the affairs and business of the world. How those things can be done, if anyone wishes to hear it from me, he must first [conjectured: sow] such seeds of speech^7 as he has received and merited. For all things are not owed to all people, but one person is to be preferred to another.

The fourth benefit is that, by enlargement of the received likeness of the thing, all those things can be extended into any language whatever, once the binary instruction^8 has been reduced to unity. Yet this is not granted to just any people one can name, but only to those persons whom God, by his special grace, and art and nature, have dignified for such things.

The fifth benefit is that, by imitation of likeness, those skilled in the art can devise, through the invention of our science, whatever secrets of our mind we wish to have hidden, in many and manifold ways, by such methods that by no other person from outside will they ever be able to be noticed. A manifold speech without voice^9 is given to them; through it, safely, securely, very widely, with every suspicion removed, we shall be able to indicate most fully to those who know the art all conceptions of our mind, whatever their difficulty. And this wonderful invention has innumerable developments, capable of every kind of mystery.^10

The sixth benefit is that, through understanding this work, you will be able to discover a free [conjectured: method of] metathesis,^11 regulated by literary transposition,^12 and nevertheless to form it in such a way that it serves only those who know the art, and absolutely no other person in the world. Great is the power of metathesis, both in form and operation; it has many modes and is varied in many ways.

The seventh benefit is that, through understanding this volume, a very great faculty is given to those desiring to enlarge [conjectured: it] without labor of memory, whenever the small seeds^7 have been placed in their proper degrees. For a good reason all things are hidden and concealed, wrapped in accepted words and figures; if anyone wishes to understand them fully, let him recall to mind [conjectured: that unremitting labor conquers all things]. For it will have been enough for me to have set down some few principles and to have handed on modest elements of symbolic striking/writing^13, rough and deliberately unformed. For there was neither time nor reason for our discoveries to be shaped with more refinement; nor did the authority of one [unclear] publish them for boys to become indignant at. [unclear] All things are untimely which do not agree with the customs and the time of the mortals among whom they are produced.

Page 027

Many very noble human talents have belonged to unsuitable times, and many new things are found almost in times not their own. What did the remarkable invention in nautical art^14 profit the outstanding [conjectured: Bartholomaeus]^15, under Pope Innocent VIII?^16 In a certain little book he offered it for sale for several thousand ducats; yet neither the pontiff himself, nor the Venetians, nor the Genoese,^17 to whom the matter thus proposed [conjectured: he had made over / submitted] in due manner, deigned to meet with him. For he promised that by his art he could preserve thirty ships in the middle of the sea, repair a broken one, and retrieve without danger whatever had been cast into the depths. But no one took care. Nor does it escape me that many, with Naso,^18 have perished by their own genius. Therefore it is better to set a limit to knowledge than, without [conjectured: advantage], to expose oneself to the hatred and detraction of many, among whom it is customary to despise anything which they have not learned.

End of the same preface, on the seventh day of April, in the year of the Lord's birth 1508.

First Book of the Polygraphia,^19 addressed to Maximilian Caesar,^20 by Johannes Trithemius,^21 abbot of [conjectured: Peapolis/Wurzburg?]^22, formerly of Sponheim.^23

^1. nosterit sub lingua materna is best read as an OCR-scanned noverit sua lingua materna; the sense is someone literate in his native language. ^2. otagi solitariis is damaged. notis solitariis is a plausible OCR reconstruction, because early print n/o and t clusters are easily lost. ^3. mythologiae is probably not classical “mythology” in the modern sense, but Trithemius's occult/signifying cover-language; the OCR is legible enough to keep the technical ambiguity. ^4. arteçi felenti appears to conceal something like arteque silenti; this is an OCR scanno plus possible compositor damage, not a secure reading. ^5. romani sermonis imperiori is a damaged form of Romani sermonis imperito, “unskilled in Latin/Roman speech.” ^6. artis nonuie discepolus = artis novae discipulus; OCR has u/n, c/e, and long-s confusions. ^7. semina/minuarii femina are Trithemian “seeds,” i.e. elementary units or principles of the art, not literal seeds; the later occurrence is badly OCR-damaged. ^8. institutione binario ad unitatem is technically important and obscure: likely a rule for reducing paired/binary instructional forms into a single transferable method. ^9. multiplex sine voce locutio, “manifold speech without voice,” is a core cipher phrase for silent communication. ^10. mystrioriae is an OCR-damaged form of mysteriorum or related; translated broadly as “mystery.” ^11. metathesis is a technical term for letter transposition, here a cipher operation. ^12. tralipofitione literariae is an OCR scanno for transpositione literaria/litteraria, “letterary/literal transposition.” ^13. feriendi symbolice may be OCR for scribendi symbolice; feriendi as transmitted is not silently corrected because the reading is uncertain. ^14. nauticae artis names nautical technology or seamanship rather than a rhetorical “art” only. ^15. The OCR has Bartholomaei; the historical referent is uncertain from this damaged excerpt. Do not identify him more specifically without external collation. ^16. Innocent VIII, pope 1484-1492; named entity and chronological anchor. ^17. lanuenses is an OCR scanno for Ianuenses, the Genoese; compared with Venetis, another maritime power. ^18. Naso is Ovid, Publius Ovidius Naso; the allusion is to a poet destroyed or harmed through his own genius, but the exact phrase is damaged. ^19. Polygraphia: Trithemius's cryptographic/steganographic work; the printed title begins after the preface here. ^20. Maximilian Caesar is Emperor Maximilian I, addressee of the work. ^21. Johannes Trithemius, Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia. ^22. Paepolitani is damaged/uncertain in the supplied OCR. It likely refers to Trithemius's later abbacy at St James in Wurzburg, but the printed form cannot be recovered securely here. ^23. Spanhenemfis is an OCR scanno for Spanheimensis/Sponheimensis, referring to Trithemius's former abbacy at Sponheim.

Audit note — v1.0 translated the wrong table range and treated cipher/nonsense entries as ordinary recoverable text, while silently inventing readings instead of marking the badly damaged colophon prose.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Third Book Closing Tables and Preface/Colophon

Cipher Tables, pp. 421-423

These lines are not continuous Latin prose but tabular cipher material: alphabetic heads paired with invented word-forms and running numbers, e.g. a damas ... 961 through zv ... 1032, then further series through zv ... 1056. I preserve them as technical nomenclature rather than translate them. Several entries show likely OCR or type damage (baschataq nan, duplicate or irregular numbers, marachost cobos, cobij, fasij, repeated vadon, etc.), but the basic tabular function is clear: they are substitution or nomenclator entries in the Polygraphia.^1

Page 424

[unclear] in the beginning of the third [book] of the Polygraphia.^1

In this work of ours we had promised [conjectured: to provide] [unclear: glossae?] by shadow and similitude,^2 [unclear: for those inexperienced in copying the work], with enough [unclear] along with an example. Secret things by night are struck or effected safely; with shadows [unclear: a paraphrase/roundabout expression] is to be led by agreed forms,^3 and the numbers, set between in the order of four lines,^4 adapted throughout to the use and will [of the user].

The places are degrees of small divisions,^5 having [conjectured: sixty thousand one hundred fifty] [or: [unclear]], although, if you wish, the moments of hours are also infinite, for concealing in every nation and language of the world whatever secret matter occurs.^6 You will be able to bring back the linearly-born circle from the point,^7 as often as night exceeds the image of light, to whatever things you have wished, and whenever there is need, by the path by which you came. If much of night remains over, with the dragon’s tail brought back to the original tail-place, [bring it] into the head.^8 But let the binary be altogether certified from the notes and signs of unity.^9

He who hungers for much should labor much, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is it a matter of great labor to lead back into the roll what has gone forward of its own accord.^10 Here, therefore, we set the end of the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.^11 Gentle reader, farewell. From [unclear: Peapoli/Spanheim?], on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh indiction.^12

Here is the end of the third book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of [unclear: Peapoli/Spanheim?], of the Order of Saint Benedict.^13

^1. Polygraphia is Trithemius’s steganographic and cryptographic work; the preceding pages are alphabetic cipher/nomenclator tables, not ordinary Latin sentences. ^2. OCR damage: glofaenonve is not secure Latin. It may point toward glossae or a related technical term, but the printed reading cannot be recovered confidently from this OCR alone. ^3. periphraenum and comfimis are likely OCR scannos for forms involving periphrasim/periphrasin and consimilis/confirmis or similar; translation keeps the uncertainty. ^4. ordine quatuor linearum is a cipher-layout term: the order of four lines or rows in the table/mechanism. ^5. Minutiae and gradus are technical division terms, probably referring to fine cipher positions or steps, not physical “places” in the ordinary sense. ^6. fcretandis is an OCR scanno for secretandis or similar: “for making secret / concealing.” ^7. “Circle born linearly from a point” appears to be technical-geometrical cipher language; it is obscure authorially as well as damaged by OCR. ^8. cauda draco[nis] = “tail of the dragon,” a traditional astronomical/astrological term for a lunar node, here probably repurposed as cipher-directional language. caudalicium is uncertain and may be OCR-corrupt. ^9. Binarius, notae, signacula, and unitas are technical terms here; the sense seems procedural, but the exact operation is not recoverable from the damaged text. ^10. uoluerie is likely OCR for volumine or a related word (“roll/book/volume”), but the reading is conjectural. ^11. Trinitarian closing formula: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. ^12. “Indiction” is a late antique and medieval fifteen-year fiscal dating cycle; the given date is March 7, 1508. ^13. Johannes Trithemius was a Benedictine abbot. Peapolitani is not secure; it may be an OCR corruption of a place-title. The expected historical association may be Sponheim/Spanheim, but that cannot be silently substituted from this OCR line.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Book IV: Damage-Preserving Translation

Heading

The fourth book of the Polygraphy^5 of Johannes Trithemius^1, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater Apostle at Würzburg^2, formerly of Sponheim^3, of the Order of Saint Benedict^4, begins.

Preface

The order of the reasoning demanded that the fourth book of our Polygraphy should be [conjectured: more difficult] than the preceding ones in quality, invention, and ease; so that those [source reads “not/wishing,” probably damaged: conjectured: wishing] to share in the secrets of our matters might attain this not by one method, but by various and different methods.

We have extended a [unclear; conjectured: practice/method] comprehensible by an easy invention, so that [unclear: night/voice?], through minuteness, always joined to the monad^7, may be recognized in any order in the light of day. No [unclear; conjectured: distinction] is found between unity and the binary^7, nor will it be necessary for a person instructed in the art^10 and wishing to operate to have [it] at hand, since the first will follow without an intermediary, and the hidden thing is [conjectured: shown] in the mysteries.

Therefore the prudent person, intelligent and experienced in the science^10, [unclear; conjectured: will be able], at every time and place, [unclear; conjectured: to work quite easily]. The binary is [conjectured: received] from unity, whence the ternary^7 is [conjectured: produced]. The first knowledge is easy [unclear; conjectured: from the face of this prologue]; afterwards the moon, or a single point, will have been illuminated by the sun.^8 Any industrious person may [unclear; conjectured: become gnostic/skilled and able to do this] without the guidance of a master.

This, however, is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning the following books, judgment will be given in its own place. Among all the cabalistic^6 methods of secrets that we have given up to the present, the progression of this fourth book can more easily be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and, at the same time, the cause of the example. The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things.

Written at [conjectured: Neapolis?]^9, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Pages 426-429: Cipher Tables

The following material is not continuous Latin prose but a set of cipher alphabet / nomenclator-like tables^10 keyed to letters a-z and zv. The entries are left untranslated. OCR damage may affect individual artificial words, especially where f/s, c/e, n/u, and v/u are confused.^11

Page 426 begins: a Baldach a hanasar a cathai ... zv Evenalach zv skvadamar zv ozvanisar.

Page 427 begins: a malach a dabam a caman ... zv ovamelech zv ezvalman zv ezvalt.

Page 428 begins: a manias a baron a sadiel ... zv tuwilas zv puvalon zv evariel.

Page 429 contains three further alphabetic series, beginning a nasor, a paranas, and a nabet, and ending respectively zv dunefoz, zv uwaras, and zv vuebrat. The final l ij appears to be a foliation or signature marker rather than part of the cipher table.^12

^1. Johannes Trithemius: Johann Tritheim/Trithemius, Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia; the heading’s IOAN-TRITEMII is an OCR/typographic form of his Latin name. ^2. Saint James the Greater Apostle at Würzburg: VUIRICBURGENSIS is an OCR/early-print spelling for Würzburg/Wirciburgensis; MA-IORIS divides Maioris across a line. ^3. Sponheim: SPANBEI-MELIS is a damaged form of Spanheimensis, “of Sponheim,” Trithemius’s former abbacy. ^4. Order of Saint Benedict: DNI BENEDICTI abbreviates Domini Benedicti. This is a normal early-modern abbreviation, not authorial obscurity. ^5. Polygraphia: Trithemius’s cryptographic work. POLYGRA-PHICE reflects line division and the Greek/Latin title form; translation uses “Polygraphy.” ^6. “Cabalistic”: here a technical label for secret or combinatorial cryptographic methods, not necessarily Jewish Kabbalah in a strict theological sense. ^7. Monad, unity, binary, ternary: technical number-language for the cipher’s combinatory structure. Several surrounding verbs are OCR-damaged, so the arithmetic relation is clearer than the exact syntax. ^8. Moon, sun, and point: likely metaphorical/technical cipher language for illumination or marking; the sentence is damaged enough that the mechanism should not be over-specified. ^9. Peapolis: likely OCR for Neapoli or another place-name, but the source form is too damaged for certainty. The date noua die Martii is almost certainly nona die Martii, “ninth day of March”; Ooeauo is OCR for Octavo. ^10. “Art,” “science,” and cipher tables: Trithemius regularly calls cryptographic procedure an ars or scientia. The alphabetic lists are artificial cipher vocabulary, not ordinary lexical Latin. ^11. OCR scannos: examples include faebice probably for fabricae/differentiae contextually, diffensio for differentia, nequopterbit for neque oportebit, babere for habere, reçpore for tempore, and tradiffc finiul for tradidisse simul. ^12. l ij: probably a printer’s gathering/signature or folio indication. It should not be translated as part of the prose or cipher alphabet.

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: unrecoverable_blocks_present; OCR quality: 5/5.

Audit note — V1.0 correctly sensed the opening but silently compressed a huge corrupt repetition into a single [unclear], hiding that the transmitted text is mostly unrecoverable mechanical duplication.

Clavis Polygraphiae — damaged decipherment commentary / preface

Damaged Latin Passage

“Whence / from which he might perceive^1 that he could not come to terms, or associate, with his own people^2: with certain persons hostile to him,^3 with certain persons his enemies, with certain persons his his enemies, with certain persons his his his enemies [continuing in a mechanically repeated series: inimicis suis followed by ever more repetitions of suis], [unclear].

The remaining block is not coherent Latin prose as transmitted. It consists almost entirely of the repeated formula quibusdam inimicis suis suis suis... with the possessive suis accumulating line by line, and then breaks off at quibusdam inimicis sui. I have not normalized this into a meaningful sentence.”

^1. vndeprehenderet is probably an OCR run-on or scanno for unde deprehenderet / unde prehenderet: “whence he might perceive/discover.” The reconstruction is plausible but not certain. ^2. convenire cum suis can mean “come together with his own people,” “agree with his own people,” or “associate with his own party/household.” Context is insufficient to choose narrowly. ^3. inimicis means “enemies” or “hostile persons”; in this damaged context it may be social/political rather than strictly military. The repeated possessives after it are textual/OCR corruption, not interpretable syntax.

Clavis Polygraphiae: Table of Reverse Transposition

Table of reverse transposition^1

[Cipher table preserved as OCR text; several letterforms are visibly unstable, especially w/3/z, u/v, and b/h.]^2

w 3 y x u t s r q p o n m l k i b g f e d c b a w

p o n m l k i b g f e d c b a w 3 y x u t s r q p o

Commentary

In this [conjectured: true] reverse table^3 you have, through the transposition of letters,^4 as many alphabets^5 as we also registered in the preceding straight table.^6 For you perceive that under [conjectured: metathesis/metabasis]^7 there were [unclear] of those going to the right,^8 and likewise as many of those going to the left; [conjectured: twenty-three] downward,^9 and [conjectured: twenty-three] upward.^10 These, multiplied by [unclear] four-and-twenty times, and reduced in the fashion of a cross^11 to four sides, make not fewer than [unclear] alphabets.

The same table follows, expanded.^12

^1. Tabula transpositionis auerca: read aversa, “reversed / turned back”; an OCR or type-reading confusion of s as c is likely. ^2. The table is a cipher alphabet grid, not prose. OCR has probably confused early-modern letterforms: 3 may represent z; u may stand for v; OCR b may be printed h in places. These are scannos, not authorial obscurity. ^3. hacuero is almost certainly hac vero, “in this, indeed / in this true”; rendered minimally as “[conjectured: true]” because the OCR has fused words. ^4. transpositioni literarui is read as transpositionem litterarum, “transposition of letters.” The case ending is OCR-damaged. ^5. alphabeta: technical term for the several cipher alphabets generated by shifting or reversing the character sequence. ^6. precedente quoq recta coisignauimus: read praecedente quoque recta consignavimus, “we also marked in the preceding straight [table].” ^7. metabesi may be metathesi or metabasi; both are technical Greek-derived terms for shifting/transfer. The exact printed word is not secure. ^8. dextrorum: “of those to the right,” i.e. rightward letter shifts or transpositions. ^9. deorium xxiiiq. is probably deorsum xxiii, “downward, twenty-three”; q may be punctuation or abbreviation noise. ^10. furium. xxiiiq. is probably sursum xxiii, “upward, twenty-three”; initial long-s misread as f is a common OCR scanno. ^11. in modi crucis: read in modum crucis, “in the manner/form of a cross,” referring to four directional arms of the transposition scheme. ^12. expania: read expansa, “expanded.” OCR has confused s with i or lost the nasal/letterform.

Audit note — V1.0 treated the damaged numeric tables as clean data and silently normalized uncertain prose/title readings, masking OCR column corruption and unrecoverable letter-form details.

Johannes Trithemius to the Reader: Numeral Letters

Address

Johannes Trithemius,^1 abbot [unclear: PEAPQ / LITANVS],^2 sends greeting to the reader.

Prefatory Explanation

Since the letters of the Greeks^3 and Hebrews^4 are all numeral, I have often wondered that the curious Latin usage of the ancients did not also make its own letters subscribe to numbering. The Hebrews, by doubling certain letters [unclear], established twenty-eight signs sufficient for every number. The Greeks also, because of a defect in [their] letters, supplied it with like prudence by the addition of four characters.

Since we, therefore, have twenty-four letters, why do we not also make our letters numeral? Likewise we can discover four doubled forms. Let us give four in examples, and this will be enough for every number: final m and n [unclear]; likewise final r and s; likewise long f and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u.^5 When these are added to the twenty-four usual letters, we shall have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers.

Therefore it is no matter of great labor to grasp the business of numbering and the method, for those who know these letters, if they have once commended them to memory. For this brief invention of ours can be useful to many, since with few letters it embraces many thousands in number; all these can be discerned and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. This, especially in large numbers, seems to many persons less experienced in the art of calculation not to be so easily possible by the figures of algorism.^6 For as soon as you have cast your eye on a number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. And so that this may be easy, we shall gather together the letters themselves reduced to number. Written 16 March, in the year 1507.^7

Page 483: Order of the Numeral Letters

The heading reads: “Order of the numeral letters.”^8 The following table assigns Latin letters, letter-pairs, and special letter-forms to numerical values. The OCR is damaged in the columns and repetitions, so the sequence should be treated as a transcriptional witness rather than a corrected table. It begins: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, e = 5, f = 6, g = 7, h = 8, i = 9, k = 10; then ka = 11 through ki = 19; l = 20 through li = 29; m = 30; ma = 31 through [unclear] = 50; n = 51 through ni = 59; o = 60 through oi = 69; p = 70 through pi = 79; q = 80 through qj = 90; and r / ra etc. continue the series. Several entries are visibly corrupt or duplicated: mi is printed as 40, nj forms appear for the forties, nd appears twice at 54, r and qj both appear as 90, rg skips to 97, and the thousand-series contains repetitions such as wc = 1003 and inconsistent values for bw, ew, and nw.^9

Page 484: Further Order of Numeral Letters

The heading again gives an order of numeral letters. The table extends the notation into millions and higher powers, for example yw = 8,000,000; zw = 9,000,000; kw = 10,000,000; and later values up to kw = 100,000,000. Several entries conflict with the preceding page or with each other: kw is used both for 10,000,000 and 100,000,000, lw appears as 2,000,000 after previously appearing as 20,000, and the tw/sw/vw/uw/xw/yw/zw values are not internally stable in the OCR.^9

Behold, reader: you have the method by which you can adequately configure and write every writable number with few letters; and their extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But, as the proverb formerly [unclear: duci/used?] had it, “The ox/bull plants its foot firmly”;^10 whoever wishes to be content with prescribed limits follows the ancient method of numbering. So that those less learned may understand easily, it will not be tedious now to give in the following material the form which Hunibald the Frankish historiographer,^11 also Bede,^12 Rabanus,^13 Helpericus the monk,^14 and many of the ancients used in chronicles and ecclesiastical calculations,^15 as follows.

Page 484: The Method of Numbering of Hunibald the Frank and Others

The heading reads: “The method of numbering of Hunibald the Frank and others.” It gives ordinary Roman numerals: 1 through 20; tens from 30 to 90; hundreds from 100 to 900. The OCR preserves the older additive forms: xxxx for 40 and lxxxx for 90, and cccc / dcccc for 400 / 900, rather than the later subtractive forms xl, xc, cd, cm.

Page 485: Order of the Ancient Numeral Letters

The heading reads: “Order of the ancient numeral letters.” The table extends ancient numeral notation beyond 1,000, including entries for 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000, and higher values. Some signs are not ordinary alphabetic letters but large-number signs resembling Roman numeral symbols such as ↀ, ↁ, ↂ, and related forms.^16 Because several entries are OCR-corrupt or typographically unstable, I preserve the sense only: the table is offered as an older method for large-number notation in chronicles and ecclesiastical computation, not as part of Trithemius’s new twenty-eight-character system.

Page 486

The remaining heading is visible only as: “The ancient order of numeral letters,” with no recoverable accompanying text in the supplied OCR.

^1. Johannes Trithemius, Latinized as Tritemius here; Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia / Clavis Polygraphiae tradition. ^2. The title after abbas is badly OCR-damaged: “PEAPQ / LITANVS.” This likely reflects a place/title epithet, but the supplied OCR is not enough to restore it securely. ^3. Greek alphabetic numerals assign numerical values to letters, with extra archaic signs used for some values. ^4. Hebrew letters are used numerically in gematria-style notation. The OCR phrase around “duplicatet literāri” is damaged; the general sense is doubling or supplementing signs to reach twenty-eight. ^5. Technical typographic distinction: long f/s, final s, closed/open u/v. OCR may confuse f and long s, and closed/open forms are easy to collapse in modern transcription. ^6. Figurae algarismi: Hindu-Arabic numerals and their computational notation; “algorism” is the medieval/early-modern term for calculation with them. ^7. 16 March 1507. The date is clear despite OCR normalization issues. ^8. Ordo literarum numeralium: a technical table heading, not continuous prose. ^9. These are OCR/table-alignment problems, not authorial obscurity. The page layout has multi-column numerical lists, and OCR has merged columns, duplicated entries, and misread characters. ^10. The proverb line is damaged: “Bos taurus fortiter figit pedem.” I translate conservatively; the exact proverbial source/form is uncertain from the OCR. ^11. Hunibaldus Francus, presented here as a Frankish historiographer. The historical authority is part of Trithemius’s antiquarian apparatus and should not be silently modernized. ^12. Bede, early medieval scholar associated with chronology and computus. ^13. Rabanus, i.e., Hrabanus Maurus, Carolingian scholar and ecclesiastical writer. ^14. Helpericus / Helperic, a monk associated with computistical writing; the OCR form “Helpericus” is recoverable. ^15. Calculationes ecclesiasticae: ecclesiastical computations, especially calendar and computus calculations. ^16. Large-number Roman numeral signs are typographically vulnerable in OCR; the supplied characters may be approximate renderings of early-modern print glyphs.

Audit note — It normalizes major OCR damage into smooth Latin, especially the opening planetary-intelligence clause and Orifiel gloss, without marking conjecture or page-boundary loss.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Book Six Opening (damage-preserving translation)

[unclear: a long repeated numeric/OCR block precedes the printed page]

Page 487

The sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius,^1 abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg,^2 begins.

Before every invention and use of letters,^3 at the beginning of the world, when human beings were still uncultivated in intellect and morals, [conjectured: under the alternating rule] of the first three [conjectured: intelligences],^4 as some suppose, succeeding one another in order for one thousand and sixty-three years,^5 they were, in the sphere of the planets,^6 present in their own way to bodily things on earth through their influences.

The ancient speculators on this matter say that Saturn,^7 from the beginning of the world, presided chiefly by influence over things germinating and being born on earth, with his own ruling intelligence moderating him: this intelligence they called Orifiel,^8 that is, [conjectured: “the life-maker / life-giver of God”], for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and just as many days and hours. We report these things as poetic matters; we do not affirm them. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, the lordship of Jove is set down as assumed. After Jove, Mercury,^9 fourth in order, as ruler, adorned the minds of human beings with various arts.

Under the three intelligences just mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jove^10 were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence, whenever one person wished to announce something secret to another, he did not do it in written characters, since the office of letters was lacking, but by certain likenesses of animals, trees, and plants, or of other sensible things, according as those who had agreed among themselves did it symbolically.^11

The age of Saturn, as they say, gave human beings habits suited to the property of its influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities,^12 rough, [conjectured: forest-dwelling], sad, simple, uncultivated in life and morals, and living a long time in the flesh. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael,^13 mover of Venus, acquired [conjectured: the influence of the sphere] for three hundred fifty-four years [unclear: text breaks at page boundary].

^1. Johannes Trithemius (1462-1516), Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia. The OCR form “TRITEMII” is a normal Latinized genitive with simplified print/OCR handling. ^2. “Herbipolensis” means Würzburg. “Sancti Iacobis” should be read as Sancti Iacobi; OCR/print case damage affects the ending. ^3. “Literarum” here means letters or written characters, not “literature.” OCR damage includes INVENTIONE for expected accusative inventionem. ^4. “Intelligentiae” are planetary ruling spirits or angelic intelligences in Trithemius’s occult-chronological framework, not human intellects. ^5. The 1,063 years correspond to the first three angelic periods in Trithemius’s scheme, though the arithmetic is approximate in the damaged text. ^6. Planetary spheres/order frame the passage’s occult chronology. ^7. Saturn is the first planetary ruler in this opening sequence. ^8. Orifiel is the Saturnian intelligence. The gloss “Boc est, ju[u]ificiente Dei” is OCR-damaged; the rendering “life-giver of God” is conjectural. ^9. Mercury is associated here with arts and human ingenuity. ^10. Jove = Jupiter. OCR has “LOUE/IOEM” for Iove/Iovem, a common I/J and long-s/letter confusion in OCR. ^11. “Symbolically” renders symbolice, damaged as “LYMBOICE.” This is a recoverable OCR scanno, not a hidden German tenor. ^12. “Conditores urbium” is likely behind “CONDITORES UBIU”; OCR has dropped/blurred r and final abbreviation. ^13. Anael is the Venusian intelligence in this sequence. The final clause is cut off by the page boundary and OCR damage.

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: heavy_damage_partial; OCR quality: 4/5.

Audit note — v1.0 smoothed several corrupt clauses into fluent narrative, especially the Hichus/Pharamund chronology and the final ciphertext, without marking unrecoverable OCR loss.

Clavis Polygraphiae, decipherment commentary / preface, pp. 496-499

Damaged Opening

Even if the characters are not sufficiently beautiful and elegant, and [unclear], nevertheless it pleased me to join them, along with the new inventions of mine set down above, for the honor and reverence due to antiquity,^1 since there was no one, however slightly industrious, who could not devise prettier ones for himself according to his own judgment. Therefore this misshapen crookedness of writing [unclear] by continuous practice in writing, by easy correction, will be able to amend, and, by frequent exercise, make pleasing through habit.

Page 496

For no one, however learned or educated in any language, becomes even a good scribe^2 unless, through long habit of writing, he has changed practice into art. Another follows.

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

If anyone wishes, according to his own judgment, to fashion a new alphabet^3 for himself, two things above all must be observed; yet I do not always find these preserved in the foregoing examples. First, that he form characters easy to draw, and the simpler they are, the better they will be. Second, that he so arrange the individual letters that, when they are joined together into words, they present a beautiful and elegant face. I add a third point, not previously promised: if you wish the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, in the manner of the Hebrews.^4

Alphabet of Hichus, Ancient Bard of the Franks

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

This Hichus^5 the Frank is said to have come with Marcomer^6 from the borders of Scythia^7 to [unclear] Rhine in Germany, and to have invented these characters as a supplement to the German language; they seem to agree with it well enough in several respects.

Page 497

Pharamund^8 also, king of the Franks in Germany, the forty-third after Marcomer, who had brought in the people, died in the [conjectured: forty-sixth] year of the Lord’s nativity; when, for the purpose of invading Gaul,^9 he sent out his scouts, he found that they were writing among themselves in such characters as these.

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

Besides that alphabet of the Northmen^10 which we placed at the beginning of this sixth book, we have also found the following written out in Bede;^11 we shall set it down in letters.

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

From Latin letters too there are many alphabets: whether reduced to number according to the example which we gave in the preceding fifth book, or by another method in imitation of the Northmen, with Greek letters as well as our own, they provide a very secure way of announcing whatever we wish. Let us accordingly set down, according to number,

Page 498

the order of our usual alphabet, the letters themselves changed in an unusual way, and we shall have made a rather beautiful and elegant secret and mystical way of writing. This method of numbering, however, is different from the one we placed in the fifth book, and is more suitable to our present purpose.

[Letter-number table follows.]

Once these principles of numbering with our letters have been rightly understood, it will now be easy to carry the number to any progression whatever, just as has been shown plainly enough in the preceding books. Now let us arrange an alphabet from these.

[Alphabet arranged from the numbering table follows.]

You now have, from Latin letters, a foreign alphabet of the kind which, as we said above, the Northmen once made for themselves from Greek letters. With it, once the necessary skill has been mastered, you may write to a friend who knows the art whatever you wish for the occasion. Let us add another, which we judge safer.

Page 499

[Further alphabet / substitution table follows.]

Although in Latin speech we have no need of k, y, and w, nevertheless, because we use k and w in German, we have carried this alphabet also to the twenty-fourth number, so that it may be extended. This method of writing, too, can be multiplied and varied at pleasure.

[Ciphertext follows:] uig mgocuauvqvac; xvmmigogm3 m / mrvqm3i3m vcuigoricmym3m — according to the will of every writer.

^1. “Antiquity” here means the alleged ancient authority of the alphabets; the opening line is OCR-damaged, so the precise predicate after “beautiful and elegant” is not recoverable from this copy. ^2. Latin “scriptor” can mean writer, scribe, or copyist; here the practical art of pen-forms and handwriting is in view. ^3. “Alphabetum” in Trithemius includes artificial, cipher, and substitution alphabets, not merely ordinary ABC order. ^4. “After the manner of the Hebrews” refers to the use of duplicate or variant letter forms; the OCR “bebraeorum” is a scanno for “Hebraeorum.” ^5. “Hichus” is the printed/OCR form here; the surrounding title “HICHI” suggests a legendary Frankish “vates,” but the name should not be normalized silently. ^6. Marcomer is a legendary early Frankish leader in medieval and early-modern Frankish origin narratives. ^7. Scythia is a conventional learned toponym for northeastern/eastern barbarian origins, not a precise modern geography. ^8. Pharamund/Faramund is a legendary king of the Franks; the chronology in the OCR line is corrupt and historically fabulous. ^9. Gaul: Latin “Galli”/“Gallia” in this damaged sentence; OCR around the invasion clause is badly distorted. ^10. “Nortmanni” means Northmen/Normans; the OCR repeatedly gives recoverable letter-confusions in this word. ^11. Bede is invoked as an authority for an alphabetic form; no claim is made here that the attribution is historically secure. ^12. Several table entries contain OCR scannos or glyph loss: e.g. “Pbaramundus” for Pharamundus, “coenire” for convenire, “cõendamus” likely for commendamus or a related verb, and “fe/fch/cb” where glyphs or ligatures have been misread.

Audit note — V1 silently normalized corrupt technical terms and “inrecluctu” as fluent Latin, hiding that key cipher vocabulary and the “understanding” phrase are conjectural.

Clavis Polygraphiae, Decipherment Commentary / Preface

First Expansion Table

[The preceding alphanumeric table is a cipher table and is not translated here; its OCR state is preserved in the source.]^1

We do not expand the [conjectured: orbemata / cipher-wheels],^2 since a reason moves us: because, when it is driven farther with its own progression,^3 the immeasurable labor terrifies the mind. As for the unity,^4 which, by design, we passed over without placing it, we judge that it must be set before our additions in due order. For from those six things which we have shown by way of example, whoever is fit [conjectured: in understanding]^5 will easily attain greater things. All things are conveyed by hidden means.^6

Page 507

Second table of anomalous expansion.^7

[The alphanumeric table headed “Secunda tabula expansionis anomale” is a cipher table and is not translated here; its OCR state is preserved in the source.]^1

Whoever wishes to observe the rule of the [conjectured: orbema / cipher-wheel],^2 will have an easy and ready method of writing, and likewise of reading, the things that are secret. But whoever has transgressed the norm of the art,^8 will have toil along with his wish.

^1. The dense letter-number material is tabular cipher apparatus, not continuous prose. It should be checked against the print rather than normalized silently. ^2. “Orchemata/orbematis” is damaged or specialized cipher vocabulary. Context and the later “Regulam orbematis” support [conjectured: orbemata/orbema], probably a technical term for a rotating or ordered cipher apparatus; OCR may have confused b/h or c/b. ^3. “etagetur” is uncertain. A reading such as [conjectured: exigetur] or [conjectured: protrahetur/agetur] would yield “is carried/driven farther,” but the exact Latin is not secure. ^4. “Vnitatem” likely refers to the numerical unit, i.e., the omitted or prefixed one in the expansion scheme, not a theological abstraction. ^5. “inrecluctu” is not good Latin as printed/OCR’d. The likely intended reading is [conjectured: intellectu], “in understanding,” an OCR/scanno recovery rather than certain text. ^6. “Omnia feruntur arcanis” is terse. It may mean “all things are borne/conveyed by secrets/hidden methods”; the construction is authorially compressed, not merely OCR damage. ^7. “anomale” likely for “anomalae,” “anomalous,” agreeing with “expansionis”; light OCR or early-modern orthographic irregularity. ^8. “tranfregiturn” is damaged. The sense is probably “transgresses/has transgressed,” from “transgredi” or “transfringere”; the OCR ending is corrupt.

Damage-preserving review rendering with tenor detection and footnoting. Damage class: mid_damage_recoverable; OCR quality: 5/5.

Audit note — V1.0 translated an unrelated table/cipher page and invented continuous sense; it missed that this chunk is mostly a damaged colophon and title-page matter, not the “Order of Ternions.”

Clavis Polygraphiae / Polygraphia Closing Matter

Closing Exhortation

[unclear: many] mysteries, and the greater [conjectured: things] you will have found from these, the more ample are those that remain to be found. A road is being prepared for beginners; for those advancing along it, it will not be difficult, in the course of time, to find many things, rare things, and very great things.^1 Here one who did not know how will learn to write Latin, and prudently to wrap almost all the mysteries of his own will in a foreign [conjectured: form or idiom].^2

But so that one may understand not merely his own such mysteries which he has wrapped up [unclear: idiosa], but may also disclose the open ones, of which he has almost always until now been ignorant, the business is not one of great labor, if the paraphraser [or interpreter] of ours in this volume has fully grasped the intention.^3 For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our steganography, buried for a just reason, lest it feed unworthy babblers.^4

Indeed it had been [conjectured: foreseen / arranged] in the work that one man should not publish the work to another, but that it should be distributed by its own use alone and [unclear]. Having been wearied after a long navigation, we set our anchor here, under the name of Jesus Christ, savior of the faithful,^5 on the twenty-first day of the month of March,^6 in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1508,^7 in the eleventh Roman indiction,^8 at Paspoli [conjectured: Paspol?], a city of eastern Francia, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis.^9

End Of The Sixth Book

The end of the sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius,^10 abbot at Saint James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim,^11 of the order of the divine father Benedict,^12 is present.

Imprint

Printed with the money and at the expense of the most upright bookseller Johannes Haselberg of Aia, in the diocese of Constance,^13 in the year 1518, in the month of July.

Title Page Of The Clavis

Key of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of divine James at Herbipolis, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, of the observance of the Bursfeld fathers.^14 With privilege that it not be printed or sold by another for ten years, under the penalty as set forth in the letters. Johannes Trithemius.

^1. “prosescentibus,” “discile,” and “fucessu” are OCR scannos for proficientibus, difficile, and successu. ^2. “peregrino” is syntactically under-supplied in the OCR text; it likely means a foreign idiom, style, or disguise rather than a foreign person. ^3. “para phrastes nos tram” is recoverable as paraphrastes nostram/noster, an interpreter or paraphraser; the grammar remains damaged. “affectus inté tionem” is probably assecutus intentionem or similar, but not certain. ^4. Steganographia is Trithemius’s technical term for hidden writing. “blatteronibus” appears to mean babblers/chatterers; the form may be authorial or corrupt. ^5. Jesus Christ is named in the formal Christian dating/colophon formula. ^6. “mensis Martis” is an OCR or print form for mensis Martii, March. ^7. The stated completion date is March 21, 1508. ^8. The Roman indiction was a fifteen-year fiscal dating cycle used in medieval and early-modern documents. ^9. “Paspoli Francoru orientalisu” is heavily corrupt. “Vuiricburg” and “Herbipolim” identify Würzburg / Herbipolis in eastern Francia. ^10. Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia and Steganographia. ^11. Sponheim: Trithemius’s former abbey before his Würzburg period. ^12. The Order of Saint Benedict, the monastic order to which Trithemius belonged. ^13. Johannes Haselberg of Aia is the named bookseller/financier of the 1518 printing; “Constantiensis diocesis” is the diocese of Constance. ^14. The Bursfeld observance was a Benedictine reform congregation; “Bursfeldensiuum” is an OCR-damaged form of Bursfeldensium.
